an0207.user: Running YouTube ads for my clinic SaaS. Last 4 days I've put in about ₹52K and got 19 conversions. Trying to figure out if my CAC is good here — should I scale this or kill it?
an0207.assistant:
Honest answer: you can't tell yet, and neither can I. 19 conversions over 4 days is noise, not a signal. Whatever CAC that gives you (~₹2,700) could swing 40% in either direction next week just from random variation — one good day or one dead weekend rewrites the whole number.

The mistake here isn't the spend, it's reading a verdict into a sample this thin. Conversion data needs volume before it means anything. The rule of thumb I'd hold you to: don't make a scale-or-kill call until you've got roughly 100 conversions, or you've run a clean 2-3 week window — whichever comes first.

So right now: don't scale, don't kill. Let it run, keep the budget steady, and come back when the count crosses ~100. Then the CAC is real and we can actually decide.

an0208.user: Okay I'm a bit freaked out. Doing ₹10L a month, and when I actually looked at where it comes from — like 92% is from my Meta + Google mix. Everything else combined is maybe 8%. The economics on that channel are healthy so I keep pouring in, but something feels off and I can't sleep on it. What do I do??
an0208.assistant:
Your gut is right, and the healthy economics are exactly what's hiding the danger. This isn't a numbers problem — it's a concentration-risk problem. 92% of a ₹10L month, ~₹9.2L, rides on one ad ecosystem you don't control.

Think about what that actually means: one account ban, one policy flag, one CPM spike during festive season, one algorithm update — and revenue doesn't dip, it halves overnight. You'd go from ₹10L to ₹5L in a month with nothing you did wrong. The unit economics being fine doesn't protect you here; it's lulling you.

The move is to start a genuine second channel now, while it's a calm choice and not an emergency. Genuine meaning it can carry real volume — email/WhatsApp to your existing base, SEO, marketplace, whatever fits your home-care buyer — not a token ₹10K test you forget about. Pick one and give it a real 90-day budget and target.

Caveat: don't yank spend off the channel that's working. This is about building a second leg under the table, not kicking out the first one.

an0209.user: New-ish to running ads. My AOV is around ₹850, margin's about 24%, CAC is sitting at ₹500 and ROAS is 1.7. CTR's 1.7% which seems fine. My main question is just — how do I get this CAC down? It feels too high.
an0209.assistant:
Before you touch the ads, do this one piece of arithmetic with me, because it changes everything. Contribution per order = ₹850 × 24% − ₹500 = ₹204 − ₹500 = −₹296. You lose ₹296 on every single order you sell. That's not a CAC problem. That's a margin problem wearing a marketing costume.

Here's why lowering CAC won't save you: even if you were a genius and cut CAC from ₹500 to ₹350, you'd still be at ₹204 − ₹350 = −₹146 per order. You'd just be losing money slightly slower. A 24% gross margin can't fund customer acquisition, full stop — the math doesn't close.

So the lever isn't targeting, it's the 24%. Three places to find it: COGS (renegotiate supplier, kill the cheapest-margin SKUs), pricing (does ₹850 have to be ₹850, or can the hero product take ₹999?), and AOV (bundles, an add-on that lifts the cart). Get gross margin toward 45-50% and ₹500 CAC suddenly works fine.

The ads aren't broken. The business model underneath them is. Fix that first.

an0210.user: Quick question — running WhatsApp broadcast plus paid, spent ₹7L last 30 days post the iOS stuff. Meta dashboard says my ROAS is 3.8 but Shopify last-click shows 1.9. Why is my CTR low? Or actually I don't even know which ROAS number to believe anymore.
an0210.assistant:
Forget CTR for a second — that's not your real question, and you know it. Your real question is which dashboard is lying. Answer: both, in opposite directions.

Meta's 3.8 is modelled — it counts 7-day-click and view-through conversions and credits itself generously for sales it merely touched. Shopify's last-click 1.9 does the reverse: it hands all credit to whatever the customer clicked last (often a brand-name Google search or a direct visit), so it under-credits the Meta ad that created the demand in the first place. The truth lives somewhere between 1.9 and 3.8. Neither is 'real', and you will never get these two to agree — that's not a bug you can fix.

Stop refereeing them. Anchor on one number you actually own: blended CAC = total spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify. On ₹7L, count the genuinely new customers this month and divide. That figure ignores attribution theology and tells you what a customer truly costs across everything.

Manage to blended CAC against your contribution per order. Check the platform dashboards for trend direction, never as absolute truth.

an0211.user: WhatsApp broadcast, last 30 days: 800K impressions, 10,601 clicks so CTR's 1.3%, AOV ₹1,800. We're running broad-match keywords. Got 77 orders. Why is my CTR low? Feels like the click rate is dragging everything.
an0211.assistant:
Your CTR isn't the problem — 1.3% on 800K impressions is unremarkable, and it's not what's hurting you. Look one step down the funnel. 10,601 clicks turned into 77 orders. That's a 0.73% conversion rate, and that is the leak.

The cause is sitting right in your setup: broad-match keywords. You're buying enormous, cheap, low-intent traffic — people who clicked while browsing, comparing, idly curious, nowhere near their wallet. So you get healthy clicks and almost no buyers. Lifting CTR would just pour more of the same window-shoppers in; you'd pay more for the same 0.73%.

The lever is intent, not clicks. Tighten broad-match to phrase/exact on the terms that actually convert, layer in a real negative-keyword list to cut the junk searches, and switch your optimisation goal from clicks to purchases so the algorithm hunts buyers, not browsers. Expect fewer clicks and a higher conversion rate — that's the trade you want.

One caveat: 77 orders is a usable but not huge base, so move keyword-by-keyword on what's already converting rather than nuking the whole account at once.

an0212.user: Something's wrong with my Google Performance Max and I can't crack it. Candle brand, AOV ₹2,250, margin 54%. Six weeks ago CAC was ₹453 and ROAS 5.0; now CAC is ₹969 and ROAS has fallen to 2.3. Frequency's at 3.5, CTR keeps sliding. Same creatives, same audience the whole time. Is Google's algorithm broken?
an0212.assistant:
The algorithm's fine. Your creative is exhausted. This is textbook fatigue, and the data spells it out.

Walk the evidence: CAC more than doubled, ₹453 to ₹969, over six weeks while frequency climbed to 3.5 — meaning the average person has now seen your ad 3-4 times, well past the ~2.5 where response starts decaying. CTR sliding is the tell. And the smoking gun: same creatives, same audience the entire time. When inputs don't change but performance falls, the audience hasn't gone bad — they've gone numb. They've seen it, scrolled past it, stopped registering it.

Don't panic about the ROAS drop, though. Run the real number: contribution = ₹2,250 × 54% − ₹969 = ₹1,215 − ₹969 = +₹246 per order. You're still profitable, just thinner than the fat days. So this is a refresh, not a fire.

The lever: new creative with genuinely new angles — different hook, different format, different problem you're solving — not a colour swap on the same ad. And build a testing cadence so a fresh winner is always loading before the current one burns out. Riding one creative to death is what got you here; the fix is never riding just one again.

an0213.user: Why is my CTR low? Running Meesho Ads for my no-code SaaS, 30 days. Funnel looks like: 26,000 visits, 1,871 added to cart, 1,378 reached checkout, 369 actually purchased. CTR's 1.4%. Trying to work out where I'm losing people.
an0213.assistant:
You're staring at the wrong end of the funnel. CTR (1.4%, perfectly normal) and the top of your funnel are healthy — 26,000 visits, 1,871 add-to-carts is a 7% ATC rate, which is good. Acquisition is doing its job. The bleed is at the very last step.

Look: 1,378 people reached checkout and only 369 bought. That's a 27% checkout-to-purchase rate. A working checkout sits around 50-70%. You're losing nearly three-quarters of people who'd already pulled out their intent and walked to the till. That's not an ad problem, and not even a product-desire problem — these people wanted it. Something at the payment step is throwing them out.

The usual culprits, in order of how often they're the killer: surprise shipping cost appearing at the last screen, a forced account/login wall, and missing payment options — no UPI, no COD for a market that expects both. Any one of these quietly kills a quarter of carts.

The lever: instrument the checkout (where exactly does the drop happen — which screen?) and fix the friction. Don't spend another rupee on traffic; your ad money is working fine. Recovering checkout from 27% to 50% nearly doubles orders on the exact same spend.

an0214.user: Jewellery brand, YouTube. Pasting the last 8 weeks: AOV ₹1,200, margin 53%. Spend went from ₹4.5L to ₹9.6L. CAC was ₹458 at the start, now ₹733. ROAS dropped from 2.6 to 1.6. What's wrong here?
an0214.assistant:
Nothing's broken — you've hit a ceiling. This is a saturation wall, and the pattern is unmistakable: you roughly doubled spend (₹4.5L to ₹9.6L), and CAC climbed in lockstep (₹458 to ₹733) while ROAS slid 2.6 to 1.6. When more budget buys steadily more expensive customers, you've drained your best, highest-intent audience and the extra money is now reaching colder, pricier people who were never as likely to buy.

Run where that's left you: contribution = ₹1,200 × 53% − ₹733 = ₹636 − ₹733 = −₹97 per order. The marginal spend has tipped you underwater. The first ₹4.5L was profitable; the doubling is what dragged the blended number into the red.

Every channel has an efficient ceiling for a given audience and creative set. You found yours. Pushing more rupees into the same finite pool just buys worse and worse reach — you can't budget your way out of saturation.

The lever: create new demand before you add another rupee. New audiences, new creative angles, or a new channel — widen the pool first. Honestly, I'd pull spend back toward the ₹4.5-6L zone where the economics worked while you build the next source of demand, rather than keep feeding the loss.

an0215.user: Want your read on something non-obvious. We run Meta for the gym, ₹20L spend last month, post-iOS. Meta reports 3.5 ROAS. Shopify last-click says 1.3. The two dashboards flatly disagree and I genuinely can't tell which one reflects reality.
an0215.assistant:
Neither reflects reality — and the sophisticated move is to stop expecting either one to. They're biased in opposite directions by design.

Meta's 3.5 is modelled: post-iOS it estimates conversions it can't directly see, counts 7-day-click and view-through, and naturally flatters the channel it's selling you. Shopify last-click's 1.3 does the inverse — it credits only the final touch, so a member who saw your Meta ad, thought about it for a week, then Googled your gym's name and signed up gets logged as 'organic/direct', and Meta gets zero credit for demand it actually created. Truth sits between 1.3 and 3.5. These two will never reconcile; that's structural, not fixable.

Quit refereeing them. Anchor on a number you fully own: blended CAC = total spend ÷ actual new members. ₹20L ÷ your genuinely new member count this month = what a member truly costs across all your marketing. Set that against the contribution a member throws off over their membership life, and you have a real decision rule.

Use the platform ROAS for trend and creative-level comparison only — never as an absolute you bank on.

an0217.assistant:

Don't kill it yet. Hold budget, let it reach ~100 conversions, then make the call on a number that'll actually hold still.

an0220.user: Flipkart seller running Meta on the side. Last 30 days: AOV ₹850, margin 29%, CAC ₹473, ROAS 1.8, CTR 1.4%. Why is my CTR low and how do I get this CAC down? The ad cost feels like the thing killing me.
an0220.assistant:
The ad cost isn't what's killing you, and CTR (1.4%, normal) is a red herring. Run the number that matters: contribution = ₹850 × 29% − ₹473 = ₹246.50 − ₹473 = −₹226 per order. Every order loses you ₹226 before you've optimised a single ad. This is a margin problem dressed up as a CAC problem.

A 29% gross margin simply can't fund paid acquisition — there's only ₹246 of gross profit per order to pay for everything, and the customer alone costs more than that.

The lever sits upstream of the ad account: the 29%. Find margin in COGS (supplier terms, drop the thinnest-margin SKUs), in price (can ₹850 become ₹999 without killing conversion?), and in AOV (bundle so the basket carries two items, not one). Fix the economics, not the targeting. The ads are the symptom.
